passages.title: The Quiet Retreat from the League Table
passages.passage:
A. For the best part of two decades, the annual publication of the national school rankings was treated as a fixture of the calendar, as predictable as the examinations whose results it digested. Little did the ministry that introduced the tables imagine that it would one day be the body to bury them. Yet that is precisely what happened last spring, when, without so much as a press release, the rankings vanished from the ministry's website. In their place appeared a searchable dashboard on which no school is placed above any other.

B. It is worth recalling why the tables were created in the first place. Their champions argued that parents were choosing schools in the dark, and that a public ranking would let the sunlight in. Weak schools would be exposed; strong ones would be rewarded with applications; all of them would be pushed to improve. "Transparency was the whole argument," recalls a former adviser who helped to draft the policy. "And in a narrow sense it worked. Scores in the subjects we measured went up, year after year." She pauses before adding that narrowness was precisely the problem.

C. What the tables measured, schools taught; what the tables ignored, schools quietly dropped. Art, music and outdoor education shrank to make room for examination practice. Some schools discovered that discouraging their weakest pupils from sitting a paper did more for their position than teaching them ever could. Nowhere was this more visible than in the crowded middle of the table, where a single percentage point could move a school twenty places in either direction, and where head teachers came to feel that they were managing a number rather than a community. The tables had begun as a description of schools; before long, schools had reshaped themselves around the tables.

D. The dashboard that replaced them offers a deliberately untidy picture. Alongside examination results sit measures of pupils' progress since entry, attendance, staff turnover and the findings of an annual wellbeing survey. No composite score is calculated, and the ministry has stated that it has no intention of calculating one. Critics call the result opaque. Parents seem divided: in a survey published last month, roughly a third said they missed having "a simple answer", but fewer than one in ten said they would now choose a different school for their child.

E. Whether the reform succeeds will not be known for years, and perhaps not even then, since the question of what makes a good school has never been settled. What the episode does reveal is something about policy itself. A measure that begins as a description tends, once it carries consequences, to become a target, and a target, sooner or later, ceases to describe. Had the ministry foreseen this, it might have built its tables differently. It remains to be seen whether the dashboard, should parents ever come to lean on it as heavily, can escape the same fate.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) describes the ways in which schools changed their own behaviour in response to the rankings?
questions.explanation: Section C lists what schools did: dropping unmeasured subjects, keeping weak pupils out of examinations, and reshaping themselves around the tables.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) sets out the original case for publishing the rankings?
questions.explanation: Section B recalls the champions' argument: parents were choosing in the dark and transparency would push every school to improve.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) reports how parents have responded to the change?
questions.explanation: Section D quotes the survey in which a third of parents missed a simple answer but fewer than one in ten would choose a different school.

questions.q: Which statement best sums up the passage as a whole?
options: A ministry abolished school rankings because parents had stopped consulting them.
School rankings raised measured results but distorted schools, and their replacement may run the same risk.
The new dashboard has proved far more popular with parents than the rankings it replaced.
Transparency in education has failed and should be abandoned altogether.
questions.explanation: The passage traces the rise of the tables, the damage they did, and ends by warning that the dashboard could suffer the same fate. Parents' views are divided, and the writer never argues against transparency itself.

questions.q: What can be inferred from the way the rankings were removed (section A)?
options: The ministry was reluctant to draw attention to reversing its own policy.
The ministry's website had been redesigned for purely technical reasons.
Journalists had lost interest in the rankings many years earlier.
The removal was ordered by a court rather than by the ministry.
questions.explanation: The tables were removed 'without so much as a press release' by the very ministry that had introduced them. Quietly burying a policy you once championed suggests a wish not to publicise the U-turn.

questions.q: The word 'fixture' in section A is closest in meaning to
options: a temporary arrangement
a permanent and expected feature
a piece of sporting equipment
a controversial decision
questions.explanation: The publication is compared to the examinations themselves, 'as predictable as' them, so a fixture here is something fixed and expected in the calendar.

questions.q: The ministry plans to add a single overall score to the dashboard in the future.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Section D says no composite score is calculated and the ministry 'has no intention of calculating one', which directly contradicts the statement.

questions.q: What does the writer imply in the final sentence of the passage?
options: Parents are unlikely ever to consult the dashboard at all.
The dashboard will be withdrawn as soon as a new minister takes office.
If parents rely on the dashboard as heavily as they did on the tables, it too may start to distort schools.
The ministry secretly intends to reintroduce the tables within a few years.
questions.explanation: The 'same fate' is the one described just before: a measure that carries consequences becomes a target and stops describing. The condition 'should parents ever come to lean on it as heavily' signals that heavy reliance is what triggers the risk.

passages.title: Why Forgetting Is Not a Failure
passages.passage:
Ask most people what a good memory is and they will describe a kind of vault: things go in, stay put, and come out unchanged on demand. [1] The brain, on the evidence of the last thirty years, is less a vault than an editor, forever revising the manuscript it holds.

Consider what happens in the hours after learning. A new experience is first held in a fragile form that depends heavily on the hippocampus, a curved structure deep inside the temporal lobe. [2] During this period, and above all during deep, slow-wave sleep, the hippocampus appears to replay the day's patterns to the cortex at high speed, gradually handing over responsibility for the memory. Rats that have learned a maze show, while asleep, the very same sequences of neural firing that they showed while running it, only compressed, as though the recording were being played back on fast-forward.

What is striking is that this hand-over is never quite complete. Each time a memory is recalled, it seems to return briefly to a fragile state, open to alteration before it is stored once more. [3] The phenomenon, known as reconsolidation, goes a long way towards explaining why an eyewitness can come to remember, in perfect sincerity, details she was only told afterwards, and why a family story retold across three generations drifts so far from the events that gave rise to it.

Forgetting, too, turns out to be a far more active business than the vault picture allows. [4] Researchers have since identified cells in the hippocampus whose job appears to be exactly this: to weaken connections that are no longer being used, clearing space for the patterns that matter. Far from being a leak in the system, a certain amount of forgetting is the system working as intended.

None of this means that memory is unreliable in any everyday sense. [5] Rather, it suggests that the vault was always the wrong metaphor. What we carry is not a record of the past but a working model of it, tuned during sleep, revised at every retrieval and pruned continuously; an account that is generally good enough and occasionally, quietly, wrong.

A. Were it merely a matter of decay, old memories would all fade at roughly the same rate, which they plainly do not.
B. Anyone who has caught a cherished childhood memory in a mistake already knows how misleading that picture can be.
C. The cortex, by contrast, is thought to hold very little of what it receives for longer than a few seconds.
D. Over the following nights, however, something remarkable takes place.
E. Most of what we remember about yesterday is, after all, broadly accurate.
F. New information encountered at that moment can be folded into the original, so that the next recollection contains both.
G. Such experiments, however, have so far been carried out only on human volunteers.

questions.q: Which piece (A–G) fits gap [1]?
questions.explanation: 'That picture' in B points back to the vault image just described, and the idea that it is 'misleading' sets up the contrast in the next sentence ('less a vault than an editor').

questions.q: Which piece (A–G) fits gap [2]?
questions.explanation: D introduces 'the following nights', which 'during this period' and the reference to slow-wave sleep then pick up. Piece C also mentions the brain but 'by contrast' has nothing here to contrast with.

questions.q: Which piece (A–G) fits gap [3]?
questions.explanation: 'At that moment' refers to the fragile state on recall, and 'folded into the original' is exactly what the eyewitness example and the family story then illustrate.

questions.q: Which piece (A–G) fits gap [4]?
questions.explanation: A argues that forgetting cannot be simple decay, which is the 'more active business' just announced, and the cells that deliberately weaken connections are then offered as the alternative.

questions.q: Which piece (A–G) fits gap [5]?
questions.explanation: E concedes that everyday memory is 'broadly accurate', which supports 'not unreliable in any everyday sense' and is then qualified by 'Rather, it suggests…'.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Memory is a fixed store that only fails when the brain is damaged.
Memory is a constantly revised model rather than a permanent record, and that is how it is meant to work.
Sleep is the only period in which new memories can be formed.
Eyewitness testimony should never be accepted in court.
questions.explanation: Every paragraph attacks the 'vault' image: consolidation in sleep, alteration at recall, and active forgetting all show a memory that is edited rather than stored. The eyewitness is one example, not the thesis.

questions.q: What does the writer imply about the family story 'retold across three generations'?
options: The people who told it were deliberately embellishing it to entertain.
It changed a little at each retelling without anyone intending it to.
The original events were never properly written down.
Older family members have far more reliable memories than younger ones.
questions.explanation: The story is offered as an example of reconsolidation, in which each recall lets new details be 'folded into the original'. The eyewitness in the same sentence acts 'in perfect sincerity', so the drift is unintended, not dishonest.

questions.q: The word 'pruned' in the final paragraph is closest in meaning to
options: strengthened
copied
trimmed
concealed
questions.explanation: To prune is to cut back what is unneeded, as a gardener does. The passage has just described cells that weaken unused connections to clear space, so the memory model is being trimmed, not enlarged.

passages.title: Half a House
passages.passage:
A. On the northern edge of a coastal city stands a row of houses that, at first sight, looks abandoned halfway through construction. Each has a concrete frame, a roof, a staircase, a kitchen and a bathroom, and beside each of these sits an empty void of exactly the same size, open to the sky. Nothing has gone wrong here. The void is the design. It was left, deliberately and at some cost to the architects' reputation, for the families themselves to fill.

B. The reasoning was brutally simple. The public subsidy available for each family would buy either a small, complete house on cheap land an hour from the city, or half of a much better house in the neighbourhood where the families already lived and worked. Rather than build the whole of something poor, the architects chose to build the difficult half of something good: the structure, the plumbing, the party walls and the roof, the parts that a family with limited tools and no engineering training cannot safely construct alone. "We did not design a house," the lead architect said at the time. "We designed the hard half and got out of the way."

C. A decade on, no two houses in the row are alike. Some voids have been filled in brick, some in timber, one in a patchwork of salvaged windows. One family has built outwards to open a small shop; another has added a second storey for a married daughter. Property values along the row have risen steadily, whereas a conventional, fully finished social-housing estate a few streets away has lost value over the same period. Not every outcome is happy, though. A handful of the extensions are poorly built, two families never completed theirs, and the row has lost the visual unity that architects are trained to prize.

D. It was this last point that split the profession. To some, leaving half a house unbuilt was an abdication: handing families a problem and calling it participation. To others, self-building is simply what poorer households have always done, on hillsides and in back yards, and the scheme merely gave that instinct a safe skeleton to grow on. What the argument really turned on was not craftsmanship but the older question of who architecture is for, and whether the architect's vision should outrank the occupant's.

E. The model has since been copied elsewhere, with mixed results. Where funding rules permit it, incremental schemes have flourished; where a subsidy may be spent only on a dwelling certified as complete, the approach is impossible. Yet the row's deepest challenge is not to housing policy but to the idea of completion itself. Buildings are normally at their best on the day they are handed over and decline from there. These houses invert that curve: at hand-over they are at their least finished, and, if their architects are right, at their most useful.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) explains the financial reasoning behind leaving half of each house unbuilt?
questions.explanation: Section B weighs what the subsidy could buy: a whole poor house far away, or half of a good house where the families already lived.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) mentions a house being adapted for use as a business?
questions.explanation: Section C reports that one family 'built outwards to open a small shop'.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) describes a disagreement among architects about the scheme?
questions.explanation: Section D says the point 'split the profession' and sets the two positions against each other.

questions.q: Which section (A–E) explains why the model cannot be adopted in every country?
questions.explanation: Section E states that where a subsidy may only be spent on a dwelling certified as complete, the approach is impossible.

questions.q: What is the writer's main purpose in this passage?
options: To warn governments against spending public money on self-built housing
To examine a housing scheme that challenges the assumption that a building should be finished at hand-over
To argue that visual unity is the most important quality of a housing estate
To describe the career of a well-known architect
questions.explanation: The passage presents the scheme, its reasoning, its results and the debate it caused, then concludes that its deepest challenge is 'to the idea of completion itself'. Neither the architect's career nor visual unity is the focus.

questions.q: What does the comparison with the 'conventional, fully finished social-housing estate' (section C) suggest?
options: The finished estate was built on more expensive land.
The freedom to extend and adapt is part of what gave the half-houses their lasting value.
Fully finished housing is always of poorer construction than self-built housing.
The families in the finished estate were wealthier to begin with.
questions.explanation: The writer places the rising value of the adaptable row directly against the falling value of a finished estate nearby. The only difference the passage has drawn between them is that one could be extended by its occupants, so that is what the contrast is meant to point to.

questions.q: The word 'abdication' in section D is closest in meaning to
options: the giving up of a responsibility
a bold experiment
a generous gift
an act of rebellion
questions.explanation: The sentence glosses abdication as 'handing families a problem and calling it participation', so the critics meant that the architects had surrendered a duty that was theirs.

questions.q: The scheme has been reproduced in other places without any difficulty.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Section E says the model has been copied 'with mixed results' and is 'impossible' wherever subsidies must be spent on completed dwellings, so the statement contradicts the text.
